TI "Qualitative study on nursing students' perspective on ethical conflicts
   at the end of life: "We are not prepared"
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing students; Ethical conflicts; Euthanasia; End of life;
   Conscientious objection
ID HOSPICE NURSES; EUTHANASIA; ISSUES
AB Background: Nursing care for people at the end of life is a crucial aspect of health care that involves challenges and responsibilities. In this scenario, ethical conflicts often arise resulting in situations of great suffering and high-level emotional impact, for which nursing students do not feel sufficiently prepared. Objective: The aim of this study was to find out how nursing students perceive the ethical conflicts present at the end of life and their reflective and deliberative capacity in the face of these conflicts. Design: Descriptive qualitative study. Setting and participants: Between February and March 2023 with nursing students at the University of Huelva in Spain. Methods: Sixteen in-depth interviews were conducted. The data analysis was carried out using Giorgi's method and Atlas.ti 22 software as a support. Results: The students reported that they had encountered ethical conflicts in the end-of-life phase during their internship care period. The main causes they mention are: the management of ethical conflicts, the position on euthanasia and conscientious objection, and the influence of values and beliefs about care. They highlight the lack of training in coping and emotion management in end-of-life care. Conclusion: Nursing students feel unprepared to deal with the suffering and ethical conflicts involved in end-oflife care, as well as the management of their own internal conflicts. There is therefore a need for the implementation of high-fidelity simulation-based training that generates the learning of the necessary competencies in bioethics and defensive palliative care through appropriate competencies.

TI "A multi-pronged teaching" approach: Effects of the "IMAGE" teaching
   mode on the learning of evidence-based practice by nursing postgraduates
SO NURSE EDUCATION TODAY
LA English
DT Article
DE Nursing education; Evidence-based practice; Postgraduate nursing
   students; Interactive learning; Mixed learning; Advanced learning; Group
   learning; Electronic learning
AB Background: Although international organizations have identified evidence-based practice as a core competence for healthcare professionals, more than half of clinical nurses lack confidence in implementing and disseminating evidence-based practice. Given that postgraduate nursing students have significant potential in evidence-based practice translation, it may be an effective strategy to train future postgraduate nurses in advanced evidencebased practice competences. Objectives: The study had two primary objectives. First, it aimed to introduce the "IMAGE" teaching mode in evidence-based practice education for postgraduate nursing students. Second, the study sought to compare academic performance, evidence-based practice competency, critical thinking, cooperative ability, and satisfaction with the course among students, through the application of the traditional teaching mode versus the "IMAGE" teaching mode. Design: This study employed a quasi-experimental design. Setting and participants: The study was conducted at the Faculty of Nursing of Guangzhou Medical University, in the academic years of 2022 and 2023. The research subjects were postgraduate nursing students who participated in the evidence-based practice course. Methods: The intervention group (n = 72) received the "IMAGE" teaching mode, and the control group (n = 72) used the traditional teaching mode. Outcomes evaluated were the students' academic performance, evidencebased practice competency, critical thinking, cooperative ability, and course satisfaction. Data were collected from both groups after the implementation of the teaching modes. Results: The findings showed that the "IMAGE" teaching mode significantly improved postgraduate nursing students' overall academic performance, evidence-based practice competency, critical thinking, cooperative ability, and course satisfaction (all P < 0.05). Conclusions: The "IMAGE" teaching mode appears effective in training postgraduate nursing students in evidencebased practice. This study may offer valuable insights for nursing educators on developing innovative teaching strategies for advanced nursing students.

TI A Critical Discourse Analysis of the Resistance to the Implementation of
   Comprehensive Sexuality Education in Ghana
SO AMERICAN JOURNAL OF SEXUALITY EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Ghana; comprehensive sexuality education; critical discourse analysis;
   educational policies; CSE
ID SCHOOL
AB The decision of the Ghana Education Service to introduce comprehensive sexuality education (CSE) into its pre-tertiary education curriculum received a barrage of attacks from politicians, religious leaders, and the Ghanaian media, prompting the government to perform a U-turn on its implementation. Drawing on a dataset of 120 articles comprising news reports, op-ed pieces, and editorials, I explore the discursive strategies employed in the Ghanaian media to resist CSE implementation. I combine insights from critical policy analysis and critical discourse analysis to shed light on how, through the media, individuals and groups other than curriculum experts influence educational policies. This study draws on existing theorization of policy as the authoritative allocation of values to argue that resistance to CSE stemmed from the discrepancy between the perceived values espoused by CSE and Ghanaian traditional heteronormativity. Resistance strategies utilized included sensational headlining, framing CSE as a covert means to expose/acclimate students to LGBTQI+ lifestyles, framing CSE as a danger to Ghanaian values, framing CSE as a foreign imposition, and threatening a regime change. The findings strengthen scholarly understandings of how education policies are resisted in public discourse and the need for a broader education policy formulation process that is culturally sensitive.

TI Parents of the Gifted: A Scoping Review of the Gifted Parent Literature
SO JOURNAL FOR THE EDUCATION OF THE GIFTED
LA English
DT Article
DE family; gifted education; giftedness; parenting; literature review
ID SPECIAL-EDUCATION; CHILDREN; PERCEPTIONS; FAMILIES; IDENTIFICATION;
   TEACHERS; STUDENTS
AB This scoping review reflects on the extant research on parents of the gifted following the last critique of the literature offered by Jolly and Matthews in 2012. The method for the search followed the PRISMA-Scr protocol utilizing the SPIDER framework. Articles fell into two main themes of parental awareness and parental actions in the inductive content analysis. Using the a priori focus areas from the Jolly and Matthews article on the second-round content analysis, articles aligned with the five focus areas: examining attitudes and expectations of nontraditional families, studying the full range of satisfaction with school programming, investigating alignment of parental understanding of terms with researchers, determining how parental understandings translate into behaviors, and reviewing relationship dynamics that contribute to underachievement. There was insufficient evidence for a COVID-19 impact on publications. Findings reflect the importance of including international literature and lay the groundwork for a robust mixed-methods synthesis.

TI "I know we need to be regulated, but I don't think this is the right
   way": Early education managers' experiences of group setting inspections
   in England
SO JOURNAL OF EARLY CHILDHOOD RESEARCH
LA English
DT Article
DE early childhood; inspections; leadership; managers; Ofsted
ID EARLY-CHILDHOOD EDUCATION; TERM
AB Early childhood education is regarded as key to help ensure long-term positive outcomes for children, and high-quality provision crucial for long-term developmental outcomes. However, how settings are inspected for the quality of their services varies substantially across countries. In England, the inspection body Ofsted has been heavily criticised for its high-stakes sanction-oriented approach to inspections. This study aimed to understand what makes a high-quality setting from the point of view of early years managers, and how they experience the inspection procedure, including any challenges faced, and ideas for a different inspection framework. Interviews with 21 managers resulted in three main themes: (a) key elements of the learning environment and resources for child development, (b) key organizational aspects, and (c) moving forward. Managers recognize the need for an inspection system but are dissatisfied with the current approach. They suggest a model where more advice and more prolonged engagement with the setting results in a supportive relationship that develops staff, in line with a low stakes, advisory-oriented model.
